21.0.0.en: 1- “The king shall joy in thy strength, O Lord; and in thy salvation how greatly shall he rejoice!”

21.0.1.en: 1- Who is the king but David, who rejoices in the power of God that saved him from his enemies the children of Ammon; and in his likeness every believer who reigns by his will over himself, controlling his senses, thoughts and feelings, rejoices in the power of God that supports him in his war with the demons and saves him from them.

21.0.2.en: 2- David rejoices because the victory over the enemies is very great, despite their strength, and God saved him from them beyond human logical expectation, for the power of God surpasses the expectations of men because of His great love for His children.

21.0.3.en: 3- David saw Christ, who would become incarnate in the fullness of time, and rejoiced in His power that triumphed over Satan and in His wondrous salvation, which He would offer to mankind.

21.1.0.en: 2- “Thou hast given him his heart's desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips. Selah.”

21.1.1.en: 1- The desire of the heart is a person's inner longings and feelings, and it precedes the request of the lips, that is, the requests a person asks of God; God gave David both, for He answered the desire of his heart and his requests.

21.1.2.en: 2- God answers the desire of the heart and requests when they agree with His will.

21.1.3.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, who desired our salvation and loved us before the foundation of the world, and desired to eat the Passover with His disciples, and likewise asked the Father for our salvation and for our being kept from evil in the world (Jn 17).

21.1.4.en: 4- At the end of the verse is the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditating during it on God's love for His children, who gives them the desire of their hearts and their requests, and which encourages His children to hope and to ask of God.

21.2.0.en: 3- “For thou preventest him with the blessings of goodness: thou settest a crown of pure gold on his head.”

21.2.1.en: 1- David asked God to deliver him from his enemies and give him victory over them, and because he asked nothing for his own glory God gave him the victory, and added to it other divine blessings, which are various good things, such as wealth and the widening of his kingdom. This is what God also did with the daughter of Solomon, who asked for wisdom, and He gave it to him, in addition to wealth, so that he was the richest man of his age.

21.2.2.en: 2- David declares that these blessings go before the person who trusts in God, that is, God makes easy his way to reach the Kingdom, and makes easy also many aspects of his life, and he finds in every road he walks divine blessings awaiting him, so he feels God's hand generous to him in giving.

21.2.3.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ in His going before with blessings of goodness, for before His Incarnation God declared many prophecies and types of Him, and it was said that Abraham saw the Incarnation of Christ and rejoiced (Jn 8:56). The men of God and the prophets in the Old Testament beheld the Incarnation of Christ and rejoiced in it; these are the blessings with which God poured out upon His children in the Old Testament as a preparation for His Incarnation.

21.2.4.en: 4- God set a crown of pure gold on David's head, that is, he received material blessings and spoils in his victories, among them a very large crown of gold, belonging to the king of the children of Ammon, which they put on David's head after David's victory over the children of Ammon (2 Sam 12:30).

21.2.5.en: 5- And symbolically this crown is placed on the head of Christ and means:

21.2.6.en: A- The crown of thorns, which represents the unlimited love of Christ, which appeared in His bearing all the sufferings for the salvation of His people.

21.2.7.en: B- The crown of the Resurrection and the Ascension; that is, the glory Christ received in the declaration of His Resurrection and His ascension to the heavens.

21.2.8.en: C- This crown is the twelve Apostles, of whom the Book of Revelation tells us as the twelve stars crowning the head of the woman clothed with the sun, that is, Christ and His Church (Rev 12:1).

21.2.9.en: D- The crown is the Church, which is the bride of Christ; as a virtuous woman is a crown to her husband (Prov 12:4), so the Church is the crown of gold that Christ acquired with His blood.

21.2.10.en: 6- God set on David's head the crown of glory, which is that Christ would be born of his seed, and this is the greatest crown, that Christ is called the Son of David (Ps 110:1).

21.2.11.en: 7- The crown is the crown of virtues that God places on the head of everyone who believes in Him in His Church and strives to acquire any virtue, and God crowns him in glory.

21.3.0.en: 4- “He asked life of thee, and thou gavest it him, even length of days for ever and ever.”

21.3.1.en: 1- David was exposed to death many times, during the pursuit of Saul and Absalom and during his wars with the surrounding nations, so he asked life of God, and He delivered him and gave him life on earth, and then eternal life.

21.3.2.en: 2- This verse applies plainly to Christ, because He alone is able to live forever, and before His death He asked for life when He said, “if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Mt 26:39). And God gave Him life by His Resurrection and Ascension.

21.3.3.en: 3- This verse applies to every believer who asks for a spiritual life with God, and He gives him eternity.

21.3.4.en: 4- Life is Christ, for He said, “I am the resurrection, and the life” (Jn 11:25); whoever asks for life, that is, Christ, on earth, God gives him eternal life, as Christ said, “whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die” (Jn 11:26).

21.3.5.en: 5- David also said this verse as a prophecy about King Hezekiah, to whom Isaiah announced that he should set his house in order because he would die, so he asked life of God, and then He granted him an extension of his life of fifteen years, in addition to eternal life.

21.4.0.en: 5- “His glory is great in thy salvation: honour and majesty hast thou laid upon him.”

21.4.1.en: 1- David was the youngest of his brothers and a shepherd of sheep, and God took him and anointed him king, and magnified him with great glory, not only by his sitting on the throne of the kingdom of Judah, but also by the coming of Christ from his seed.

21.4.2.en: 2- God delivered David with great glory from the hands of his enemies, and even lifted him above them, so that the surrounding nations were subdued to him and offered him gifts and tribute.

21.4.3.en: 3- This verse is a prophecy about Hezekiah, to whom the nations came with gifts after God lengthened his life, and the Assyrians submitted to him after his victory over them.

21.4.4.en: 4- Christ emptied Himself by His Incarnation and His redemption on the Cross, so God glorified Him by the Resurrection and the Ascension, after He had bound Satan.

21.4.5.en: 5- Every believer who strives and reigns over his senses, his thoughts, his speech and his works, God blesses him and glorifies him in the eyes of people in this life, and then with great glory in eternity.

21.4.6.en: 6- If the king enjoys glory and majesty, all this is grace from God and not from man.

21.5.0.en: 6- “For thou hast made him most blessed for ever: thou hast made him exceeding glad with thy countenance.”

21.5.1.en: 1- God does not only bless the king, or Christ, or the believing spiritual striver, but makes him himself a blessing to those around him, so that everyone connected with him receives a blessing, as Abraham the father of the fathers was a blessing to all around him, and likewise Joseph in the house of Potiphar, and in prison, and on the throne of Egypt.

21.5.2.en: 2- “Thou hast made him blessings for ever”: this applies plainly to Christ, because He blesses His children who believe in Him on earth, and continues to give them the blessing forever; He is the focus of all eyes and the satisfaction of all in heaven.

21.5.3.en: 3- God gives everyone who believes in Him the grace of joy and gladness, by which he is distinguished from all around him who are troubled and wretched because of sin, because they live for the world; but the mark of God's children is joy.

21.5.4.en: 4- The cause of the joy of God's children is God's looking upon them and their fellowship with Him, for He is in them, and they rejoice at all times as long as they hold fast to Him.

21.5.5.en: 5- Joy and gladness remain in the heart of God's children by His constant care for them and their remaining before Him, but if they go away from before Him they lose the joy.

21.5.6.en: 6- The victory of the spiritual person in his wars against the demons, or the victory of the king over his enemies, makes him glad, but in order to continue victorious and in joy he must remain before God, that is, look to God as his only goal throughout his life.

21.6.0.en: 7- “For the king trusteth in the Lord, and through the mercy of the most High he shall not be moved.”

21.6.1.en: 1- The king draws his strength in governing his kingdom from God, in whom he trusted, and consequently succeeds in all his affairs, just as the person who reigns over his spirit and his body is successful by trusting in God.

21.6.2.en: 2- He who relies on God is not troubled or shaken, but whoever trusts in the world and its power must be troubled, because he is exposed to falling and the passing of his kingdom.

21.6.3.en: Why do you weary yourself and are troubled on your way to achieving success, when the way is clear before you, namely trust in God, for through Him you receive grace and peace and ability to accomplish all your affairs? So hold fast to His commandments, and cast all your labors upon Him, and He is able to use your abilities at the right time and in the right manner to bring you success.

21.7.0.en: 8- “Thine hand shall find out all thine enemies: thy right hand shall find out those that hate thee.”

21.7.1.en: 1- God promises the king that His hand will find his enemies, and will bring them down and destroy them, that is, none of them will escape, and by this the striving spiritual person is turned from one defending himself into one who overcomes and rules over his enemies the demons, as we say in the prayer of thanksgiving, “He gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy.”

21.7.2.en: 2- The king's hand strikes and so punishes the enemies, but his right hand, which symbolizes salvation, as the Psalm says of God, “The right hand of the Lord is exalted: the right hand of the Lord doeth valiantly” (Ps 118:16), strikes in order to save those who hate him, and this means that David, or Christ, or any spiritual person wants the salvation of those who hate him; if he disciplines them, he wants their salvation, as Joseph did with his brothers.

21.7.3.en: 3- If the hand mentioned in the verse means the left, this means that if the spiritual person uses his right hand and his left in striving, that is, all his works are on the way of spiritual striving, he will certainly triumph over his enemies.

21.8.0.en: 9- “Thou shalt make them as a furnace of fire in the time of thy presence: the Lord shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them.” Furnace: an oven, that is, the place where they kindle fire; it represents a huge mass of flames, whatever the kind of oven.

21.8.1.en: 1- God declares to David that his enemies burn like a furnace of fire and the fire devours them, that is, their power is destroyed, and they become as nothing. This is what David did to the children of Ammon, when he made them pass through the brick kiln (2 Sam 12:31).

21.8.2.en: 2- The fire declares God's wrath by distress, pain and the reproach of conscience in this life, and then eternal torment at the end.

21.8.3.en: 3- David's enemies are God's enemies, so in the time of God's presence the enemies burn, and this is what supports God's children, that God fights for them, and as long as He is with them all the enemies fear and are defeated, and even burn.

21.8.4.en: 4- God's wrath and anger and the fire that devours the wicked are not hatred on God's part toward them, but are the natural result of their works, which call for divine justice; the wicked have sentenced themselves by their wickedness, and deserved this destruction.

21.9.0.en: 10- “Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.”

21.9.1.en: 1- The enemies vanish from before David, or the spiritual person, or Christ, so that they have no power or effective deeds, that is, the fruits that are in the earth. By this David disregards their existence, and goes on in his positive, constructive works. Likewise the spiritual person goes on in the way of acquiring virtues, not hindered by the wars of the demons.

21.9.2.en: 2- God destroys the seed of the wicked, that is, there is no man left to weary and trouble David. And the enemies of man are sins; and sins are of two kinds: the mother sins, that is, the great, “their fruit,” and the small sins that result from them, “their seed”; God helps the spiritual person to overcome both, and this helps him to be free for positive work.

21.9.3.en: 3- The wicked who tried to kill David and his people God destroyed, that is, their sin came upon their own heads, and what they wanted to do to David came upon them. This is what happens with the demons, who fight God's children to destroy them, and God delivers them, and casts the demons into eternal torment.

21.9.4.en: 4- If the earth symbolizes the body, then our holding fast to God destroys the fruits of evil, that is, the sins into which the demons try to make us fall.

21.9.5.en: 5- This divine punishment of the wicked is a threat to them, that they may turn back from their wickedness, and it is a hard threat, because it includes their seed also; if they do not fear for themselves, their hearts may be moved because their children also will be destroyed.

21.10.0.en: 11- “For they intended evil against thee: they imagined a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform.”

21.10.1.en: 1- David's enemies tried to wrong him and do evil to him, and even set snares for him in war that he might fall into them, but God delivered him from all this, and no harm came to him.

21.10.2.en: 2- The Jews tried to wrong Christ with evil words, and tried to kill Him, and then crucified Him, but all this turned to the glory of God, for Christ by the Cross accomplished our redemption, and then rose from the dead with great power. And the Jews tried to spread the rumor that His disciples stole the body, but their attempt failed, and Christ appeared to many.

21.10.3.en: 3- The demons try to wrong God's righteous children, so they set snares for them, but God delivers them, and the demons are put to shame, and evil comes upon their own heads.

21.10.4.en: 4- While the wicked devise schemes, God frustrates them before they are completed, so although their hearts are full of evil toward God's children, their schemes fail.

21.11.0.en: 12- “Therefore shalt thou make them turn their back, when thou shalt make ready thine arrows upon thy strings against the face of them.”

21.11.1.en: Turn their back: run and flee.

21.11.2.en: Make ready: to place the arrow on the string to shoot it, meaning to aim the arrow.

21.11.3.en: 1- The strength that God gives David makes his enemies fear him and flee from before his face. So also with Christ, when they tried to seize Him and He said to them, “I am he,” they feared and went backward and fell to the ground (Jn 18:6). And God's children who hold fast to Him are feared by the demons, who flee from them, as happened with the saints who cleansed the deserts. Thus the enemies turn from attackers to fearful ones and fugitives.

21.11.4.en: 2- God aims His arrows at the wicked, that is, He threatens them that He will destroy them, that perhaps they may repent. This shows that God's justice is bound up with His mercy, for He seeks their salvation and their return to Him. But if they persist in their wickedness, punishment and destruction await them.

21.11.5.en: 3- God shows His power in His children, as they defy the wicked and stand against their faces; meaning that He gives His children courage that frightens the enemies. This appeared in David and likewise in Christ, but those who refused to believe, their wickedness came upon them.

21.11.6.en: Do not fear the wars of the demons, for they are worthless as long as you hold fast to God in the sacraments of the Church and the means of grace, and humble yourself at all times and the demons will flee from you.

21.12.0.en: 13- “Be thou exalted, Lord, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power.”

21.12.1.en: 1- If Christ emptied Himself by His Incarnation, David sees in the spirit of prophecy the Resurrection of Christ and His Ascension, and asks Christ to be exalted before those who opposed Him and crucified Him, that perhaps they may repent and believe.

21.12.2.en: 2- When God's children see His power and His victory over the enemies they rejoice and praise, singing spiritual songs; this is the conclusion of this great Psalm.

21.12.3.en: 3- If the beginning of the Psalm tells us of the power of God (v. 1), its end is also sealed with His power and exaltation, as we end the Lord's Prayer by saying, “Thine is the power, the glory and the honor.”

21.12.4.en: Do not let your heart cling to the earthly glories you achieve, because they are changing and passing, but hold fast to your prayers and to doing good. This is what remains for you, and keeps you and lets you enjoy fellowship with God.

21.12.5.en: The sufferings and glories of Christ. To the chief musician upon Aijeleth Shahar. A psalm of David. “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” ... (v. 1) Introduction:

21.12.6.en: 1- David wrote this Psalm, but the events mentioned in it did not happen in David's life; he speaks of another person, that is, he speaks of Christ in the spirit of prophecy, after God inspired him with the thoughts of Christ on the Cross and in His sufferings, and then after His Resurrection and His kingdom, and he recorded all that for us in this Psalm.

21.12.7.en: 2- It says in the title of the Psalm “upon Aijeleth Shahar,” and Aijeleth is the time of the dawn, that is, the dark time just before daybreak, and at this time the Jews used to prepare the morning burnt offering, which is a symbol of Christ, who rose early at the dawn of Sunday, and whose sufferings and Resurrection this Psalm speaks of.

21.12.8.en: And the title of this Psalm is Aijeleth Shahar (the hind of the morning) because it contains the sufferings and Resurrection of Christ, who saved us from the darkness of the night and gave us the dawn of the new life; indeed it is said of Him that He is “the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). There is another opinion that Aijeleth Shahar was a tune to which this Psalm was sung.

21.12.9.en: 3- What confirms that this Psalm is Messianic is that David did not mention in it his confession of any particular sin, or his justification of any particular sin, or ask for vengeance on his enemies; he tells us of the sufferings borne by a righteous man who committed no sin, so it applies to none but Christ. And although this Psalm speaks of the sufferings of Christ and His salvation, its title Aijeleth Shahar points to His Resurrection, because the aim of the sufferings and death of Christ is the Resurrection.

21.12.10.en: 4- This is the first Psalm in the Book of Psalms that speaks of the sufferings of Christ, and the Fathers regard it as one of the greatest Psalms that speak of His sufferings.

21.12.11.en: 5- Because this Psalm contains events that took place at the ninth hour, the Church chants it in the sorrowful tune (Adribi) at the ninth hour on Great Friday. And because it was customary that if one of the Jewish priests said the beginning of a Psalm the hearers would complete it, Christ uttered the beginning of this Psalm on the Cross at the ninth hour (Mt 27:46), so that the Jews standing beneath the Cross might complete it and know that this Psalm is a prophecy about Him, that perhaps they might believe.

21.12.12.en: 6- This Psalm declares an important truth that the Jews forgot, namely God's acceptance of the Gentiles and their salvation (vv. 27-31).

21.12.13.en: 7- This Psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
